concepts.name: The goal: make money now and in the future
concepts.one_line: A for-profit firm has one goal: make more money now and in the future.
concepts.formula: Goal = increase NP while ROI and cash flow increase at the same time.
misconceptions: Quality, efficiency, market share, technology and cost cuts are the goal.
Short-term profit alone is the goal; 'in the future' is part of it.
how_to_apply: Write the goal of the system in one line.
List what you measure now; mark each item as goal or necessary condition.
Reject any action that does not move NP, ROI or cash flow.

concepts.name: Necessary conditions
concepts.one_line: Conditions the system must keep (customer, employee, cash) to stay on the goal.
misconceptions: A necessary condition is a second goal to maximize.
Cash flow is only a measure; it is also a survival condition.
how_to_apply: List the conditions that, if broken, stop the firm.
Keep them as limits, not targets.

concepts.name: Productivity = movement toward the goal
concepts.one_line: An action is productive only if it moves the company toward its goal.
concepts.formula: Productive if delta T up or delta I down or delta OE down, with no offset.
misconceptions: Output per worker or per machine is productivity.
Robots that raise efficiency raise productivity.
how_to_apply: For each improvement, state delta T, delta I, delta OE.
If all three are zero, the improvement is not productive.

concepts.name: Global measures: NP, ROI, cash flow
concepts.one_line: Three bottom-line measures tell whether the whole firm makes money.
concepts.formula: NP = T - OE; ROI = (T - OE) / I; cash flow = cash in - cash out (survival test).
misconceptions: NP alone is enough; a high NP on a huge investment can be bad.
Cash flow matters only in a crisis.
how_to_apply: Compute NP, ROI and cash flow for the whole system, not per department.
Use T, I, OE as the operational link to them.

concepts.name: Throughput (T)
concepts.one_line: Rate at which the system generates money through sales.
concepts.formula: T = sales revenue - totally variable cost (materials, commissions); per period.
misconceptions: Production is throughput; a finished good in stock is not T.
Throughput is units per hour of a machine.
how_to_apply: Count T only at the sale.
Subtract only truly variable cost per unit.
Rank decisions by delta T first.

concepts.name: Inventory (I)
concepts.one_line: All money the system invests in things it intends to sell.
concepts.formula: I = raw material + WIP + finished goods + (in later TOC) equipment and buildings, at purchase cost only.
misconceptions: Inventory is an asset, so more is fine.
Labor and overhead are part of inventory value.
how_to_apply: Value inventory at raw-material cost, no added labor.
Track WIP in front of each resource as a signal of flow problems.

concepts.name: Operating expense (OE)
concepts.one_line: All money the system spends to turn inventory into throughput.
concepts.formula: OE = all wages, rent, energy, depreciation; a mostly fixed cost per period.
misconceptions: Direct labor is a variable cost per unit.
Cutting OE is the main lever to profit.
how_to_apply: Treat labor as a fixed cost per period.
Before an OE cut, check its effect on T.

concepts.name: Local efficiency fallacy
concepts.one_line: Keeping every resource busy raises inventory and OE, not throughput.
concepts.formula: Sum of local optima is not the global optimum.
misconceptions: High efficiency at each machine means a good plant.
Idle workers are waste.
how_to_apply: Find each local measure that rewards busy time.
Replace it with a measure tied to T, I or OE.
Allow non-bottleneck idle time.

concepts.name: Cost world vs throughput world
concepts.one_line: Cost world cuts cost everywhere; throughput world protects T at the constraint first.
concepts.formula: Priority: T first, then I, then OE.
misconceptions: Every saved cost goes to the bottom line.
Product cost per unit tells which product to push.
how_to_apply: Before a decision, compute delta T, delta I, delta OE.
Ignore allocated product cost.

concepts.name: Inventory reduction hits reported profit
concepts.one_line: Cutting WIP releases absorbed overhead, so reported profit drops for a period.
concepts.formula: Absorption cost: overhead in inventory moves to cost of sales when stock falls.
misconceptions: A lower reported profit after inventory cuts means the plant got worse.
Inventory valuation is a neutral fact.
how_to_apply: Tell finance before a WIP cut.
Report T, I, OE next to the cost report for the change period.

concepts.name: Dependent events
concepts.one_line: A step cannot start until the steps before it finish.
misconceptions: Each step can be optimized alone.
A late step can always catch up.
how_to_apply: Draw the sequence of steps.
Mark which steps wait for which.

concepts.name: Statistical fluctuations
concepts.one_line: Every step has variable output; in a chain, delays add and gains do not.
concepts.formula: Output_k = min(capacity_k, input available_k); E[min] <= min of means.
misconceptions: Variation averages out over time.
Plan with averages and the line meets the average.
how_to_apply: Measure the spread, not only the mean, of each step.
Put protection (buffer) where it protects throughput, not everywhere.

concepts.name: Matchstick (dice) game
concepts.one_line: Five dependent stations roll dice; line output falls below the average roll.
concepts.formula: Each round: station k moves min(die roll, matches waiting). Mean roll 3.5; line output < 3.5; WIP grows.
misconceptions: A balanced line with mean 3.5 per station gives 3.5 per round.
Lost output is the fault of slow workers.
how_to_apply: Run 20 rounds with 5 stations, 1 die each.
Plot cumulative output vs 3.5 x rounds and WIP per station.
Repeat with one slower station and a rope.

concepts.name: Herbie hike
concepts.one_line: The slowest walker sets the speed of the whole troop.
concepts.formula: Troop speed = speed of slowest walker; gap length = inventory.
misconceptions: The fast walkers at the front set progress.
Making every walker faster helps.
how_to_apply: Put the slowest step at the front (release at its pace).
Take load off the slowest step.
Tie the line so gaps cannot grow.

concepts.name: Balanced plant fallacy
concepts.one_line: Matching each capacity exactly to demand guarantees missed shipments and high inventory.
concepts.formula: Balance the flow, not the capacity (OPT rule 1).
misconceptions: Remove all excess capacity to cut cost.
Non-bottleneck spare capacity is waste.
how_to_apply: Keep spare capacity on non-bottlenecks.
Size capacity so fluctuations do not starve the constraint.

concepts.name: Bottleneck
concepts.one_line: Resource whose capacity is equal to or less than the demand placed on it.
concepts.formula: Bottleneck if load hours >= available hours for the period.
misconceptions: The busiest-looking resource is the bottleneck.
A bottleneck is bad; remove all of them.
how_to_apply: Compare load to capacity for each resource.
Confirm with WIP queues in front of it.
Confirm it is not a shortage made by bad release.

concepts.name: Non-bottleneck
concepts.one_line: Resource whose capacity is greater than the demand placed on it.
concepts.formula: Non-bottleneck utilization is set by another constraint (OPT rule 2).
misconceptions: A non-bottleneck should run at 100%.
Idle time at a non-bottleneck is a loss.
how_to_apply: Let non-bottlenecks wait for work.
Use their spare time for smaller batches and setups.

concepts.name: Capacity-constrained resource (CCR)
concepts.one_line: A resource near full load that becomes a bottleneck if badly scheduled.
concepts.formula: CCR if load is close to capacity (e.g. > 85-90%) or if bad timing makes it starve the bottleneck.
misconceptions: Only one resource can limit the plant.
A CCR has spare capacity, so ignore it.
how_to_apply: List resources with high load.
Schedule CCR work so the bottleneck buffer stays full.

concepts.name: Hour lost at bottleneck = hour lost for the system
concepts.one_line: Bottleneck time lost is throughput lost forever for the whole plant.
concepts.formula: Cost of 1 bottleneck hour = system T per hour (book first estimate: total OE / bottleneck hours).
misconceptions: A bottleneck hour costs its own machine rate.
Lost bottleneck time can be recovered later.
how_to_apply: Log every lost bottleneck minute and its cause.
Price it at system T per hour.
Fix the largest cause first.

concepts.name: Hour saved at a non-bottleneck is a mirage
concepts.one_line: Saving time at a non-bottleneck only adds idle time.
concepts.formula: Delta T from non-bottleneck time saved = 0.
misconceptions: Every setup saved anywhere saves money.
Faster machines anywhere raise output.
how_to_apply: Before a speed-up project, check if the resource is a bottleneck.
Spend non-bottleneck time on more setups and smaller batches.

concepts.name: Activation vs utilization
concepts.one_line: Running a resource (activation) differs from using it for throughput (utilization).
concepts.formula: Utilization = activation that contributes to T. Activating a non-bottleneck beyond bottleneck demand only builds I.
misconceptions: A running machine is a productive machine.
Efficiency reports measure utilization.
how_to_apply: Release work to non-bottlenecks only at the pace of the constraint.
Measure non-bottlenecks on schedule adherence, not hours run.

concepts.name: Setup, process, queue, wait time
concepts.one_line: Part lead time is setup plus process plus queue plus wait time.
concepts.formula: Lead time = setup + process + queue + wait; queue dominates at bottleneck, wait dominates at assembly feeds.
misconceptions: Process time is most of lead time.
Faster machines cut lead time most.
how_to_apply: Measure the four times for one part.
Attack queue and wait, not process time.

concepts.name: Process batch vs transfer batch
concepts.one_line: Move parts in small transfer batches; size process batches by setup cost at constraints.
concepts.formula: Halve batch size -> about half WIP and half lead time (Little's Law at constant T).
misconceptions: Big batches are efficient.
Transfer batch must equal process batch.
EOQ gives the right batch size.
how_to_apply: Cut transfer batches first; they cost little.
Cut process batches at non-bottlenecks; spare time pays for setups.
Keep bigger batches at the bottleneck only if setups eat its time.

concepts.name: Quality control before the bottleneck
concepts.one_line: Inspect parts before the bottleneck so it never works on bad parts.
concepts.formula: Scrap after the bottleneck costs bottleneck time; scrap before costs only materials.
misconceptions: Inspect at the end of the line.
Scrap cost = material cost.
how_to_apply: Move inspection to the input of the constraint.
Give extra care to parts after the constraint.

concepts.name: No idle time at the bottleneck
concepts.one_line: Keep the bottleneck running through breaks, shift changes and setups.
misconceptions: Breaks and shift rules are fixed.
Idle bottleneck time is small and harmless.
how_to_apply: Stagger breaks so the constraint never stops.
Keep a buffer of work in front of it.
Stage setups while it runs.

concepts.name: Offload the bottleneck
concepts.one_line: Move bottleneck work to old machines, other routes or vendors.
concepts.formula: Offload is worth it if delta T > delta OE, even at a higher unit cost.
misconceptions: An old slow machine is not worth running.
Outsourcing costs more per part, so it loses money.
how_to_apply: List parts that can run on another resource.
Compare delta T to delta OE, not unit cost.

concepts.name: Red and green priority tags
concepts.one_line: Mark bottleneck parts red so every station works them first.
concepts.formula: Rule: red (bottleneck) parts before green parts at every non-bottleneck.
misconceptions: A tag rule alone schedules the plant.
More priorities give more control.
how_to_apply: Tag work that feeds the constraint.
Watch for green work starved into a new bottleneck.

concepts.name: Drum-Buffer-Rope (DBR)
concepts.one_line: Constraint sets pace, time buffer protects it, rope ties material release to it.
concepts.formula: Release date = constraint start date - buffer time.
misconceptions: DBR needs a detailed schedule of every resource.
More buffer is always safer.
how_to_apply: Schedule the constraint (drum) by due date.
Set a time buffer before it.
Release material one buffer ahead of the drum.

concepts.name: Time buffer
concepts.one_line: Planned time between release and the constraint so variation does not starve it.
concepts.formula: Buffer is time, not units; first estimate in later TOC = half the current lead time.
misconceptions: A buffer is a pile of stock in front of each machine.
Buffers are waste to remove.
how_to_apply: Set buffers at the constraint, at assembly and at shipping.
Size by time; tune by buffer penetration.

concepts.name: Rope (material release)
concepts.one_line: Release material only at the pace the constraint consumes it.
concepts.formula: Release when order date - buffer <= today.
misconceptions: Release early to keep workers busy.
Release whenever material is in stock.
how_to_apply: Stop releasing by work-center efficiency.
Release by constraint schedule minus buffer.

concepts.name: Constraint shift
concepts.one_line: After you break one constraint, or release too much, the constraint moves.
misconceptions: Once found, the bottleneck stays.
A shortage at a non-bottleneck means it needs more capacity.
how_to_apply: Recheck load after each change.
Check if a new shortage comes from release rules.

concepts.name: Nine OPT rules
concepts.one_line: Nine scheduling rules from OPT that the plot shows one by one.
concepts.formula: 1 balance flow; 2 non-bottleneck use set by others; 3 activation != utilization; 4 bottleneck hour lost; 5 non-bottleneck hour mirage; 6 bottlenecks govern T and I; 7 transfer != process batch; 8 process batch variable; 9 schedule all constraints at once.
misconceptions: OPT is the software, not the rules.
The rules are only for factories.
how_to_apply: Check your plan against each rule.
Fix the first rule you break.

concepts.name: Five focusing steps
concepts.one_line: Identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat; do not let inertia become the constraint.
concepts.formula: 1 identify; 2 exploit; 3 subordinate; 4 elevate; 5 if broken go to 1, beware inertia.
misconceptions: Elevate first: buy capacity.
Steps are a one-time project.
how_to_apply: Name the constraint.
Get more from it with no money; subordinate all else.
Only then buy capacity; then recheck.

concepts.name: Step 1: identify the constraint
concepts.one_line: Find the one element that limits system throughput now.
misconceptions: The constraint is always a machine.
Many constraints limit a system at once.
how_to_apply: Check load vs capacity, WIP queues, and market demand.
Check policies that limit flow.

concepts.name: Step 2: exploit the constraint
concepts.one_line: Get maximum throughput from the constraint with what you have.
misconceptions: Exploit means work people harder.
Exploit needs investment.
how_to_apply: Stop all idle time at the constraint.
Do only needed, good parts on it.
Pick product mix by T per constraint minute.

concepts.name: Step 3: subordinate everything else
concepts.one_line: All other resources serve the constraint decision, even if they idle.
misconceptions: Subordinate means low priority.
Non-constraints keep their efficiency targets.
how_to_apply: Tie release to the constraint.
Change local measures that conflict.

concepts.name: Step 4: elevate the constraint
concepts.one_line: Add capacity to the constraint: machines, people, shifts, vendors.
misconceptions: Elevate is the first step.
Elevation never moves the constraint.
how_to_apply: Elevate only after exploit and subordinate.
Predict where the constraint moves next.

concepts.name: Inertia
concepts.one_line: Old rules made for an old constraint become the new constraint.
misconceptions: Once a fix works, keep it forever.
Inertia is people being lazy.
how_to_apply: After each constraint move, review the rules made for the old one.
Set a date to recheck.

concepts.name: Policy constraint
concepts.one_line: A rule, measure or habit that limits throughput more than any machine.
misconceptions: Constraints are physical.
Policies are fixed by head office.
how_to_apply: List measures and rules that drive local behavior.
Trace each to its effect on T, I, OE.
Use an evaporating cloud to break the worst one.

concepts.name: Market constraint
concepts.one_line: When capacity exceeds demand, the market limits throughput.
misconceptions: More sales effort is the only fix.
A plant with idle capacity is a failure.
how_to_apply: Use short, reliable lead time as the offer.
Sell spare capacity where it does not cut existing prices.

concepts.name: Selling spare capacity at a lower price
concepts.one_line: A low-price order pays if T is positive and OE stays flat.
concepts.formula: Accept if price - TVC > 0 and capacity spare and no effect on existing market prices.
misconceptions: Price below 'product cost' is a loss.
Low prices in one market always spoil all markets.
how_to_apply: Compute T of the order.
Check constraint time it uses.
Segment the market.

concepts.name: Short lead time as competitive edge
concepts.one_line: Reliable short lead time wins orders without price cuts.
misconceptions: Lead time is fixed by the industry.
Fast delivery needs more stock.
how_to_apply: Measure current lead time and due-date performance.
Quote a lead time you can meet with buffer.

concepts.name: Process of ongoing improvement (POOGI)
concepts.one_line: Improvement is a repeated cycle aimed at the constraint, not a project.
misconceptions: Improve everything a little.
Improvement is cost cutting.
how_to_apply: Run the five steps as a loop.
Each loop, ask the three questions again.

concepts.name: Socratic method
concepts.one_line: Lead people with questions so they build and own the answer.
misconceptions: Giving the answer is faster.
Questions are a trick to manipulate.
how_to_apply: Ask about the effect, not the solution.
Let people find the cause.
Accept their wording for the answer.

concepts.name: What to change, to what, how to cause the change
concepts.one_line: Three questions that drive any system improvement.
concepts.formula: What to change -> CRT; to what to change -> EC + FRT; how to cause the change -> PRT + TT.
misconceptions: Start with the solution.
Change needs only a good idea.
how_to_apply: Find the core problem.
Design the solution and check its side effects.
Plan the steps and the obstacles.

concepts.name: Management skills Alex seeks
concepts.one_line: A manager must find core problems, build solutions and cause change.
misconceptions: Management is a list of techniques.
Charisma causes change.
how_to_apply: Write the system's undesirable effects.
Use a method, not intuition, to link them.

concepts.name: Layers of resistance
concepts.one_line: People resist change in ordered layers; answer them in order.
concepts.formula: Disagree on problem; on direction; on solution effect; fear side effects; obstacles; unspoken fear (variants list 6-9 layers).
misconceptions: Resistance is irrational.
One good argument removes all resistance.
how_to_apply: Agree the problem first.
Then the direction, then the solution.
Then side effects and obstacles.

concepts.name: Thinking Processes (TP)
concepts.one_line: Logic trees to answer what to change, to what, and how.
misconceptions: TP is only for factories.
The trees are drawings, not logic.
how_to_apply: Pick the tree for the question you are at.
Check each arrow with the CLR.

concepts.name: Undesirable effect (UDE)
concepts.one_line: A negative effect you see now in the system, stated as fact.
misconceptions: A UDE is a missing solution ('we lack X').
Every UDE needs its own fix.
how_to_apply: Write 5-10 UDEs as present facts.
Remove items that say 'lack of'.

concepts.name: Current Reality Tree (CRT)
concepts.one_line: Cause-effect tree from UDEs down to a few root causes.
concepts.formula: Read: if [cause] then [effect]; a core problem causes >= 70% of UDEs.
misconceptions: Root cause = the bottom of any branch.
More boxes means better analysis.
how_to_apply: List UDEs.
Link with sufficient cause arrows; add AND groups.
Find the cause that feeds most UDEs.

concepts.name: Evaporating Cloud (EC)
concepts.one_line: Five-box diagram of a conflict; break it by challenging an assumption.
concepts.formula: A objective <- B need <- D want; A <- C need <- D' want; D conflicts D'. Injection removes one arrow's assumption.
misconceptions: A cloud needs a compromise.
Assumptions are facts.
how_to_apply: Write D and D' (the conflict).
Write needs B, C and common objective A.
List assumptions under each arrow; find an injection.

concepts.name: Injection
concepts.one_line: A new action or fact that makes a desired effect true.
misconceptions: An injection is the full solution.
An injection must be possible today.
how_to_apply: State the injection as a done fact.
Test it in an FRT.

concepts.name: Future Reality Tree (FRT)
concepts.one_line: Tree that shows injections lead to desired effects, with no new problems.
misconceptions: If the FRT looks good, the plan is done.
Only positive effects count.
how_to_apply: Start from injections.
Build up to desired effects (inverse UDEs).
Check for negative branches.

concepts.name: Negative Branch Reservation (NBR)
concepts.one_line: Tree that shows how a proposed action can cause a new undesirable effect.
misconceptions: An NBR kills the idea.
Raising an NBR is opposition.
how_to_apply: State the action and the feared effect.
Build the cause chain between them.
Add an injection that trims the branch.

concepts.name: Prerequisite Tree (PRT)
concepts.one_line: Lists obstacles to an objective and the intermediate objectives that overcome them.
misconceptions: Obstacles are reasons not to start.
Order of steps is obvious.
how_to_apply: List obstacles to the injection.
Write an intermediate objective per obstacle.
Order them by dependency.

concepts.name: Transition Tree (TT)
concepts.one_line: Step-by-step actions, each with need, reason and expected effect.
misconceptions: A TT is a task list.
The reasons can stay implicit.
how_to_apply: For each step write need, action, effect.
Check each effect is sufficient for the next step.

concepts.name: Categories of Legitimate Reservation (CLR)
concepts.one_line: Eight rules to test any cause-effect statement.
concepts.formula: Clarity; entity existence; causality existence; cause insufficiency; additional cause; cause-effect reversal; predicted effect existence; tautology.
misconceptions: CLR is for attack.
Only the author checks the tree.
how_to_apply: Read each arrow aloud: if ... then ... .
Test it against the eight categories.
Fix the arrow, not the person.

concepts.name: Buffer management
concepts.one_line: Prioritize and improve by how much of each buffer is used.
concepts.formula: Penetration = time used / buffer; green < 1/3, yellow < 2/3, red > 2/3, black > 100%. Resize: red share > 10% grow buffer; < 5% shrink.
misconceptions: Every red order is an emergency.
Buffer size is fixed.
how_to_apply: Color every order by penetration.
Work red first.
Pareto the causes of red; fix the top one.

concepts.name: Simplified DBR (S-DBR)
concepts.one_line: DBR with the market as drum and one shipping buffer.
concepts.formula: Release = due date - shipping buffer; promise date = planned load on CCR + half the buffer.
misconceptions: S-DBR ignores the CCR.
S-DBR is only for make-to-stock.
how_to_apply: Set shipping buffer at about half of current lead time.
Release by due date minus buffer.
Promise dates from the planned load.

concepts.name: Critical Chain (CCPM)
concepts.one_line: Project schedule on resource-dependent longest chain with aggregated buffers.
concepts.formula: Cut task estimates to about 50%; project buffer about 50% of chain (about 1/3 of project time); feeding buffers at merges; fever chart.
misconceptions: Critical chain = critical path.
Cutting estimates means people work harder.
how_to_apply: Level resources and find the chain.
Move task safety into a project buffer.
Track buffer used vs chain done.

concepts.name: Replenishment and dynamic buffer management
concepts.one_line: Hold stock centrally and refill to actual consumption, not forecast.
concepts.formula: Target up 1/3 if too long in red; down 1/3 if too long in green.
misconceptions: Push stock to stores by forecast.
Bigger orders cut cost.
how_to_apply: Set target = max consumption in reliable lead time x paranoia factor.
Refill daily what was sold.
Adjust targets by buffer color.

concepts.name: Throughput accounting
concepts.one_line: Decide with T, I and OE instead of allocated product cost.
concepts.formula: NP = T - OE; ROI = (T - OE)/I; productivity = T/OE; investment turns = T/I.
misconceptions: TA is a full GAAP replacement.
Product cost tells product profit.
how_to_apply: For a decision, list delta T, delta OE, delta I.
Accept if delta NP > 0 and ROI up.

concepts.name: Product mix: P&Q example
concepts.one_line: Rank products by throughput per constraint minute, not by margin.
concepts.formula: Rank by (price - TVC) / constraint minutes. P&Q: P 45/15 = 3 per B-min beats Q 60/30 = 2.
misconceptions: Make the product with the highest price or margin first.
All products earn the same per hour.
how_to_apply: Find the constraint.
Compute T per constraint minute per product.
Fill demand in that order.

concepts.name: Strategy and Tactics tree
concepts.one_line: Tree that links a goal to the strategy and tactics at each level.
misconceptions: An S&T tree is an org chart.
Tactics need no reason.
how_to_apply: State the strategy for each level.
Give each tactic its necessary and sufficient assumptions.

concepts.name: Little's Law
concepts.one_line: Average WIP equals throughput times average lead time.
concepts.formula: L = lambda x W (WIP = TH x CT), for a stable system.
misconceptions: Faster machines cut lead time most.
It needs a specific distribution.
how_to_apply: Measure WIP and throughput.
Compute lead time = WIP / TH.
Cut WIP to cut lead time at constant T.

concepts.name: Kingman (VUT) equation
concepts.one_line: Queue time explodes as utilization nears 100% with variability.
misconceptions: Busy resources with no wait are possible.
Variability only adds a little delay.
how_to_apply: Estimate u, ca, cs for a station.
Cut u or variability where queue is large.

concepts.name: Cost of delay and WSJF
concepts.one_line: Prioritize work by delay cost divided by duration.
concepts.formula: WSJF = cost of delay / duration (on the constrained resource).
misconceptions: First in, first out is fair and good.
Value alone sets priority.
how_to_apply: Estimate cost of delay per week for each item.
Divide by duration on the constraint.
Do highest first.

concepts.name: WIP limits
concepts.one_line: Cap work in process so flow and lead time stay under control.
concepts.formula: Pull new work only when WIP < limit; DBR rope is a WIP limit tied to the constraint.
misconceptions: WIP limits idle people, so they cost money.
The limit is set once.
how_to_apply: Set a limit per stage or per system.
Pull only when below limit.
Tune by lead time.
